paragraphs: Active learning studies how a learner can choose which examples to have labeled. In the pool-based setting considered here, the learner selects its requests from a collection of available examples. The paper asks how many label requests a particular algorithm needs, making the cost of obtaining labels the central object of analysis.

The authors study the A2 algorithm in the agnostic PAC framework. Agnostic learning allows for the possibility that the available prediction models cannot perfectly explain the labels. A label-complexity guarantee therefore has to address learning without assuming that some candidate model makes no errors. The contribution is a general upper bound on the algorithm’s label requests in this setting.

The abstract identifies this as the first nontrivial, general-purpose upper bound for agnostic PAC active learning. Its significance is a theoretical guarantee about label requirements for an existing algorithm. An upper bound limits the requests needed under the framework; it does not establish that every problem needs that many labels or that the bound is the smallest possible.
icml-2007-a-bound-on-the-label-complexit.tldr: The paper derives the first nontrivial general-purpose upper bound on label requests for A2 in agnostic PAC active learning.

paragraphs: Clustering and dimension reduction are closely connected: the representation of data affects which groups appear distinct, while the groups suggest which features of a representation are useful. This paper brings these two tasks into one framework, combining K-means clustering with linear discriminant analysis, or LDA, to select a subspace that separates the discovered groups.

K-means supplies the class labels that LDA uses for subspace selection. Those labels come from the clustering itself, allowing a method normally associated with labeled groups to participate in discovering a useful representation. Clustering and subspace selection are integrated, so the framework selects the feature subspace while also grouping the data.

The authors examine variants of this LDA-Km framework and explain their relationships to earlier approaches. This analysis also clarifies connections among principal component analysis, LDA, and K-means. Experiments on real-world datasets support the effectiveness of the combined approach. The contribution is both a practical method for adapting a representation to clustering and a framework for understanding how several familiar techniques relate.
icml-2007-adaptive-dimension-reduction-u.tldr: The paper integrates K-means and discriminant analysis so that clustering and selection of a discriminative subspace proceed together.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to predict a molecule’s binding affinity to a target protein from its three-dimensional structure. Its approach combines discovering useful molecular substructures with building the regression model that predicts affinity. This connects the choice of molecular features directly to the prediction task.

Two components drive the method. Multiple-instance regression represents each molecule through a set of three-dimensional conformations, allowing several possible configurations to enter the representation. Relational learning discovers substructures, and the Score As You Use method selects them according to whether they improve the regression model. The paper presents this as the first application of that selection method to multiple-instance prediction with real-valued outputs.

Evaluation on three tasks supports each component and their combination. Score As You Use selects regression features more effectively than standard coverage measures, while the multiple-instance representation improves accuracy over single-vector encodings. Combining the two is more accurate for the studied structure-based affinity prediction tasks than either alone. These findings support jointly considering molecular representation and predictive usefulness when constructing features.
icml-2007-an-integrated-approach-to-feat.tldr: Combining multiple molecular conformations with prediction-guided substructure selection improves binding-affinity prediction across three evaluated tasks.

paragraphs: Actor-critic learning connects a policy that chooses actions with a critic that evaluates them. This paper develops a Bayesian version in which the critic represents uncertainty about the value of taking an action in a state. Its central aim is to turn that uncertainty into information about how to update the policy.

The critic uses Gaussian process temporal difference learning to model state-action values. After observations arrive, Bayes’ rule produces a posterior distribution over possible value functions. With suitable choices of the covariance kernel and policy parameterization, the authors derive closed-form expressions for the posterior distribution of the policy gradient, which describes how the average discounted return changes with the policy parameters.

The posterior mean supplies the gradient estimate used to update the policy. The posterior covariance provides a measure of how reliable that update is. This couples a proposed direction of improvement with an assessment of uncertainty about that direction. The closed-form result depends on the specified compatibility between the kernel and policy representation, rather than applying automatically to every actor-critic design.
icml-2007-bayesian-actor-critic-algorith.tldr: Bayesian critics yield policy-gradient estimates and uncertainty measures, with closed-form posteriors under suitable kernel and policy choices.

paragraphs: K-means can process large clustering problems efficiently within each iteration, yet reaching a solution may require too many iterations. This paper addresses that distinction between the cost of a single step and the cost of finishing the clustering process. Its goal is to accelerate convergence while retaining much of the computational economy of K-means.

The proposed enhancement adds local search using swap operations resembling those in K-medoids, a clustering heuristic described as more robust. The method carefully limits the number of swaps. That control is central to the design: additional search is intended to make useful progress without greatly raising the average computational cost of an iteration.

The authors report empirical improvements in convergence compared with standard K-means. These results support the proposed combination of inexpensive K-means iterations and a controlled amount of more exploratory local search. The method remains a heuristic, and the stated finding concerns its observed convergence behavior. Its practical contribution is a way to improve progress per iteration while keeping the extra work limited.
icml-2007-best-of-both-a-hybridized-cent.tldr: Adding a controlled number of K-medoids-like swaps empirically improves K-means convergence without greatly increasing average iteration cost.

paragraphs: A model may need to work in a new domain even though most available labeled examples come from a related old domain. Because the two domains can have different data distributions, the old examples cannot simply be treated as perfectly representative of the new task. At the same time, collecting enough new labels can be expensive.

The paper introduces TrAdaBoost, a transfer-learning framework that extends boosting. It combines a small amount of labeled data from the new domain with a much larger collection from the old domain to build a classifier for the new data. The purpose is to make existing labeled information useful when the new examples alone are insufficient for training an accurate model.

The authors provide theoretical and empirical analysis of the iterative method and report that it can converge well to an accurate classifier. They show that effective transfer is possible even with very little newly labeled data. The finding establishes the potential value of combining related domains in this framework; it does not claim that any old dataset will be useful for any new task.
icml-2007-boosting-for-transfer-learning.tldr: TrAdaBoost adapts boosting to combine abundant old-domain labels with a small amount of new-domain data for accurate target-domain classification.

paragraphs: Learning systems that predict sequences can use the Viterbi algorithm during training or classification. The paper introduces CarpeDiem as a faster way to carry out that computation while retaining the optimality of the result. Here, the application called SSL is supervised sequential learning, where the predictions concern a sequence.

The key contribution is the combination of improved time complexity and preservation of the optimal answer. Computational savings therefore do not come from accepting a suboptimal result. Because Viterbi can be part of both learning and prediction, improving this computation has implications for systems at either stage, wherever the proposed algorithm applies.

The authors describe CarpeDiem in detail and show its application to supervised sequential learning, specifically the HMPerceptron algorithm. They also present experiments supporting the approach. Taken together, the stated complexity improvement and empirical evidence make this a contribution to the computational side of sequence learning: a central inference operation can become faster while preserving the quality criterion that the original algorithm guarantees.
icml-2007-carpediem-an-algorithm-for-the.tldr: CarpeDiem improves on Viterbi’s time complexity while preserving optimality, with an application to supervised sequence learning.

paragraphs: UCT learns action values through sample-based search performed online. Temporal-difference learning can also produce a value function offline from the distribution of experience generated by a policy. This paper explores how knowledge available before search and estimates gathered during search can work together.

The authors examine three approaches. One uses an offline value function to guide Monte Carlo simulations. Another combines UCT’s value estimates with a rapidly obtained online estimate of action values. The third places offline values into the search tree as prior knowledge. These approaches introduce additional information at different points in the search process.

Experiments in 9-by-9 Go against GnuGo 3.7.10 reveal that placement matters. Offline-guided simulation beats random simulation but performs worse than a weaker handcrafted simulation policy. The rapid online estimate outperforms UCT, and learned tree priors outperform handcrafted priors. The techniques are also combined in MoGo, where each significantly improves playing strength. The mixed simulation result shows that a stronger standalone source of value information need not make a better simulation policy.
icml-2007-combining-online-and-offline-k.tldr: Combining learned values with UCT improves Go performance, but the benefit depends on how that knowledge enters the search.

paragraphs: In some collective labeling problems, a group’s score depends on how many members receive a particular label. The paper exploits this count-based structure to design efficient inference algorithms for graphical models. The central question is which forms of group scoring permit exact solutions and which require approximation.

The authors give exact algorithms for arbitrary cardinality-based clique potentials with binary labels. For multiple labels, exactness is established for max-like and majority-like potentials. The distinction matters because efficient exact inference is tied to the particular family of potentials. The paper also proves that inference becomes NP-hard even for cliques with homogeneous Potts potentials.

For the harder setting, the authors provide a 13/15 approximation guarantee with runtime growing less than quadratically in clique size. They contrast this with a previously known guarantee of 0.5 for graphs with Potts potentials. Experiments on real and synthetic data show their methods running an order of magnitude faster than tree-based reparameterization and graph-cut algorithms. The contribution combines exact methods, a hardness boundary, and a stronger approximation result.
icml-2007-efficient-inference-with-cardi.tldr: Count-based clique structure enables efficient exact inference for several potential families and a strong approximation for a harder Potts setting.

paragraphs: Conditional log-linear models are used to predict structured outputs, making efficient parameter training an important computational problem. This paper develops an exponentiated-gradient method for learning those parameters. Its focus is on improving optimization of the model’s maximum-likelihood objective.

The authors apply exponentiated gradient to the convex dual of that objective, an alternative optimization formulation. This produces two algorithms: one with sequential updates performed in an online fashion and another with parallel updates. They prove convergence for both. Their analysis also simplifies earlier exponentiated-gradient results for max-margin models and yields a tighter bound on convergence rates.

On a large-scale parsing task, the proposed method converges much faster than conjugate-gradient and L-BFGS approaches. The reported advantage appears both in the optimization objective and in test error, connecting progress in training to predictive performance. The paper therefore contributes an optimization method, formal convergence analysis, and task-based evidence of faster learning. The experimental speed advantage is established for the evaluated parsing task, while the convergence proofs address the algorithms themselves.
icml-2007-exponentiated-gradient-algorit.tldr: Exponentiated-gradient training has proven convergence and converges faster than conjugate gradient and L-BFGS on the evaluated parsing task.

paragraphs: Sparse principal component analysis seeks a linear combination of variables that explains substantial variance while using only a limited number of nonzero coefficients. The paper starts from a sample covariance matrix and addresses this trade-off across all possible numbers of selected variables. This gives a range of solutions with different levels of sparsity.

The authors formulate a new semidefinite relaxation and derive a greedy algorithm that computes a full collection of good solutions. Its computational complexity is O(n³), where n is the number of variables. Producing the whole path allows the amount of explained variance to be considered alongside how many variables a solution uses.

The same relaxation yields sufficient conditions for a proposed solution to be globally optimal, with checks also costing O(n³). Passing these conditions certifies optimality; their being sufficient does not mean that every optimal solution must pass them. Experiments on toy examples and biological data show globally optimal solutions in many cases. Thus, the method combines practical candidate generation with a way to certify some of its results.
icml-2007-full-regularization-path-for-s.tldr: A cubic-time greedy method generates sparse PCA solutions across sparsity levels, with sufficient conditions that can certify global optimality.

paragraphs: Supervised prediction can involve outputs such as images, text, or graphs, whose structure is more complicated than a single number. This paper proposes a gradient-boosting framework for problems where the loss is defined through a kernel over outputs. The kernel provides a way to formulate prediction error in these more complex spaces.

The framework extends boosting to a general class of base learners that operate in kernelized output spaces. This separates the overall boosting construction from a single choice of prediction model. In the experiments, the authors use tree-based base learners and examine the resulting method on regression, image completion, and graph prediction.

Across those experiments, gradient boosting significantly improves the underlying learners. It also produces competitive results against other tree-based ensembles built using randomization. These findings support the usefulness of the framework for the evaluated output types without establishing superiority over every ensemble approach. The broader contribution is a principled route for applying gradient boosting when output similarity and loss are expressed through a kernel.
icml-2007-gradient-boosting-for-kerneliz.tldr: A kernel-based output formulation extends gradient boosting to complex predictions and improves tree learners in three evaluated problems.

paragraphs: Estimating several probability distributions becomes difficult when each dataset contains few observations. This paper considers datasets organized into overlapping groups, including hierarchies, and uses those relationships to share predictive information. The aim is to estimate the distributions jointly while making systematic use of similarities among datasets.

The authors develop a maximum-entropy formulation that incorporates the grouping structure. They derive general performance guarantees and show that hierarchical shrinkage and hierarchical priors arise as special cases. This makes the framework a connection among existing approaches as well as a proposed method for sharing information across related estimation problems.

The method is demonstrated on synthetic data and on geographic distributions of species grouped by taxonomy. The real-world application covers the Australian wet tropics and Northeast New South Wales, where limited observations per species hinder prediction. Combining information across taxonomic groups produces substantial benefits. The result illustrates why group structure can be valuable: related datasets can contribute evidence when separate estimates would each have little data to draw on.
icml-2007-hierarchical-maximum-entropy-d.tldr: A maximum-entropy framework shares information across overlapping groups, improving species-distribution estimation when observations per species are scarce.

paragraphs: A learned distance function determines which examples count as similar, affecting methods such as nearest-neighbor classification. This paper develops an information-theoretic approach to learning a Mahalanobis distance. It seeks a distance that satisfies specified constraints while minimizing a measure of difference between two multivariate Gaussian distributions.

The authors express the problem as minimizing LogDet divergence under linear constraints, placing it within Bregman optimization. The formulation accommodates a broad range of constraints and can optionally include prior information about the distance function. The resulting algorithm avoids eigenvalue computations and semidefinite programming, supporting the paper’s claim of a fast, scalable method.

An online version extends the approach to sequential learning, and the authors derive regret bounds for that algorithm. They evaluate metric learning for nearest-neighbor classification on standard datasets and in Clarify, a software error-reporting system. The contribution combines a flexible way to express distance requirements with computational advantages and an online formulation. The abstract reports these evaluations without specifying a comparative accuracy outcome.
icml-2007-information-theoretic-metric-l.tldr: Information-theoretic metric learning fits constrained Mahalanobis distances efficiently, supports optional priors, and has an online version with regret bounds.

paragraphs: Clustering constraints provide information about how data should be grouped. The paper places them in several roles: enforcing particular groupings, supplying starting information to clustering algorithms, and learning distance functions that are subsequently used for clustering. These uses make constraints part of both the definition of a grouping problem and the procedure used to solve it.

The authors investigate the computational difficulty created by combining constraints. They establish intractability results for some combinations, showing that additional requirements can make the clustering problem hard to solve. The qualification matters: the stated results concern particular combinations, rather than every use of constraints or every constrained clustering task.

The paper examines the implications through both formal reasoning and experiments. This links complexity results to the practical question of how constraints are used in clustering. Its contribution is to show that guidance about desired groups also has computational consequences. Understanding the interaction among requirements is therefore part of assessing a constrained clustering method, alongside considering what information those requirements convey.
icml-2007-intractability-and-clustering-.tldr: The paper proves that some combinations of clustering constraints are intractable and examines the consequences formally and experimentally.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised learning uses labeled and unlabeled examples together, often relying on assumptions about clusters or the geometric structure of the data. This paper proposes a regularization framework that incorporates both kinds of assumption within a kernel machine. It also makes kernel selection part of learning.

The optimization jointly considers all labeled and unlabeled examples, choices from a convex set of basic kernels, and possible labels for the unlabeled examples. Thus, choosing the representation and assigning unknown labels are coupled decisions. The presence of a convex kernel set does not make the whole search purely continuous, since the unknown labels occupy a discrete space.

When incorporating the manifold assumption, the method uses graph Laplacian kernels as its building blocks and learns an optimal convex combination of them. This provides a way to adapt the kernel within the proposed framework. Comparisons with related methods on the USPS dataset produce results described as very promising. The evidence supports the combined approach on that dataset, while the main methodological contribution is the integration of assumptions and kernel selection.
icml-2007-kernel-selection-forl-semi-sup.tldr: The framework combines cluster and manifold assumptions while jointly learning kernel combinations and labels for unlabeled examples.

paragraphs: A ranking can put two items in the correct order while losing information about how strongly one is preferred. This paper studies learning methods that aim to preserve both the ordering and the size of preference differences. Search engines and movie recommendation motivate this richer prediction objective.

The authors describe several algorithms and analyze their generalization error using stability bounds. Stability concerns the sensitivity of learning to changes in training data, providing a route to understanding performance beyond the examples used for fitting. The analysis extends earlier stability results to non-bipartite ranking and to algorithms designed to preserve preference magnitudes.

Experiments compare the proposed algorithms across several datasets, including comparisons with a method that minimizes pairwise ordering mistakes and with standard regression. These alternatives provide reference points for studying the importance of preserving rating differences alongside order. The abstract does not identify a single winning algorithm. The paper’s stated contribution is the formulation, algorithmic analysis, and empirical comparison of ranking methods that retain information about the strength of preferences.
icml-2007-magnitude-preserving-ranking-a.tldr: The paper develops ranking algorithms that preserve preference strength as well as order, with stability-based generalization bounds and empirical comparisons.

paragraphs: Data represented by many input coordinates may lie on a much lower-dimensional manifold. Algorithms that exploit this geometry often need to know the manifold’s dimension first. This paper develops a dimension estimator intended to benefit from the same underlying low-dimensional structure.

The method uses nearest-neighbor techniques to estimate dimension locally around individual data points, then combines those estimates. The authors analyze its finite-sample behavior, addressing what can be learned from a limited collection of observations. Their central theoretical result is that the estimate’s convergence rate does not depend on the dimension of the surrounding input space.

This independence is the sense in which the estimator is manifold-adaptive. When the supporting manifold is low dimensional, the method can be exponentially more efficient than alternatives that fail to exploit that property. The claim is conditional on that favorable structure, rather than a universal efficiency statement for every dataset. Computer experiments confirm the reported theoretical results, supporting the connection between local geometric estimation and improved efficiency.
icml-2007-manifold-adaptive-dimension-es.tldr: A nearest-neighbor dimension estimator has a convergence rate independent of ambient dimension and can be exponentially more efficient on low-dimensional manifolds.

paragraphs: Feature selection is especially important when a classification dataset contains very few examples but thousands of measured variables. The paper uses microarray-based cancer classification as a motivating case. It studies how to choose useful features when the available sample is small relative to the number of possible inputs.

The proposed method uses a minimum reference set generated under the nearest-neighbor rule. This is the smallest collection of examples that correctly classifies all training examples under that rule. The authors connect this compact reference set to structural risk minimization and use it as the basis for feature selection, linking the method to their argument for good generalization.

The comparison is with recursive feature elimination, which draws on support vector machines and is commonly used for small-sample problems. Across several real datasets, the minimum-reference-set approach achieves better classification performance. These experiments support using the reference-set criterion for feature selection in the evaluated setting. The finding concerns predictive performance on those datasets, rather than a guarantee that the method will outperform recursive feature elimination everywhere.
icml-2007-minimum-reference-set-based-fe.tldr: Feature selection based on a minimum nearest-neighbor reference set outperforms recursive feature elimination on several real datasets.

paragraphs: Manifold learning is often framed as placing observed data into a lower-dimensional space. This paper instead emphasizes learning a representation that can support operations on new points. It considers nonlinear manifolds, including those for which a distance-preserving unrolling is not assumed, and places generalization beyond the training data at the center of the task.

Drawing on supervised-learning ideas, the authors establish a framework for assessing models, controlling model complexity, and selecting among manifold representations. They also extend Locally Smooth Manifold Learning, or LSML, and show that it has good generalization properties. The learned representation can describe either one manifold or a family of related manifolds.

The representation supports several operations: computing distances along a manifold, projecting points onto it, recovering it from noisy observations, and generating new points on it. These capabilities explain why learning a reusable model matters beyond producing an embedding of an existing dataset. The paper connects the geometry of a learned manifold with questions about how well that representation works on previously unseen points.
icml-2007-non-isometric-manifold-learnin.tldr: The paper treats manifold learning as reusable representation learning and extends LSML to support generalization and operations on novel points.

paragraphs: A Markov decision process can describe decisions in an uncertain, changing environment, but its own parameters may also be uncertain. Parameters estimated from data, learned through experience, or specified by hand can differ from the true system. Consequently, a strategy’s actual performance may depart substantially from what its designer expected.

The paper proposes a percentile-based criterion for choosing strategies under this parameter uncertainty. The criterion expresses a trade-off between optimistic and pessimistic assessments of possible performance. The authors also describe tractable methods that incorporate uncertainty into decision making, making uncertainty part of strategy selection itself.

The approach extends to exploration when resources can be spent on actions that reduce uncertainty about model parameters. Those resources may be money, time, or computation. The authors propose a cost-effective exploration strategy for this setting. The connection is that learning about the model can itself be a decision with a cost: exploration is useful insofar as reducing uncertainty helps subsequent choices justify that investment.
icml-2007-percentile-optimization-in-unc.tldr: A percentile criterion balances optimism and pessimism in uncertain MDPs and supports resource-aware exploration to reduce parameter uncertainty.

paragraphs: Relationships in a cell or social community can change over time, so a single fixed network may miss part of the system’s behavior. This paper studies networks whose connections evolve and may not be directly observable. The available evidence instead consists of measurements associated with individual nodes over time.

The authors introduce hidden temporal exponential random graph models to represent and recover these changing networks. Inputs can include time series of social actors’ activities or gene expression levels. The modeling task is to infer the hidden topology at particular times from those observed attributes, connecting changes in node measurements with changes in the underlying relational structure.

The paper reports that latent time-specific network structures can be inferred reliably and presents experiments on synthetic data and a Drosophila lifecycle gene-expression dataset. The evaluations include a static counterpart of the proposed model. This comparison addresses the value of explicitly modeling temporal rewiring. The stated contribution is a model-based route from observable node histories to otherwise hidden, evolving network connections.
icml-2007-recovering-temporally-rewiring.tldr: Hidden temporal graph models recover evolving network structures from time series of node attributes, with evidence from synthetic and gene-expression data.

paragraphs: Spectral methods such as Laplacian Eigenmaps provide tools for discovering low-dimensional structure in nonlinear data. This paper identifies a shortcoming called the repeated eigendirections problem, in which the resulting embedding directions can repeat underlying directions of variation. The issue matters when constructing a representation that captures the manifold’s geometry.

The proposed method builds successive one-dimensional spectral embeddings and combines them with a data-advection scheme. Together, these components are designed to address repeated eigendirections. The method does not rely on nonlinear optimization, so it avoids the local-minimum problem associated with such an optimization procedure.

Experiments on artificial and real datasets illustrate advantages over existing approaches. The authors also demonstrate successful learning of manifolds affected by substantial noise, directly addressing the difficulty of nonlinear dimension reduction with noisy observations. These findings provide empirical support for the successive-embedding construction. The absence of nonlinear optimization explains one computational advantage, while the experiments provide the evidence for the method’s ability to recover useful geometry under noise.
icml-2007-robust-non-linear-dimensionali.tldr: Successive one-dimensional spectral embeddings with data advection address repeated eigendirections and recover manifolds under substantial noise in experiments.

paragraphs: Messages generated from the same template can form recognizable batches. This paper studies detecting those batches so that spam recognition can use information about related messages collectively. Because examples of correct groupings can be collected, the task is formulated as supervised clustering.

The computational focus is decoding: turning a learned clustering model into decisions about which messages belong together. Existing decoding procedures are cubic in the number of instances. The authors show that decoding can instead be performed in linear time when the streaming setting requires decisions to be final once made. That restriction is central to the efficiency result.

The paper develops a sequential decoding procedure and derives the corresponding supervised-clustering optimization problem. It also studies how attributes of whole email batches affect spam recognition. The contribution therefore connects a learning formulation with the operational demands of arriving messages. Its efficiency claim applies to irreversible sequential decisions, while the application examines how identifying shared message structure can supply collective information for recognizing spam.
icml-2007-supervised-clustering-of-strea.tldr: Supervised email-batch clustering admits linear-time decoding when streaming decisions are irreversible, enabling study of collective information for spam recognition.

paragraphs: A publication repository records papers and citations, but a citation alone does not describe how strongly one paper influenced another. This paper aims to visualize the development of a research area by tracing topics between papers, estimating influence, and helping identify contributions that shaped subsequent work.

The authors construct a probabilistic topic model that explains document generation through both topical innovation and inheritance through citations. This allows a paper to introduce material while also drawing on the topics of cited work. The distinction gives the model a basis for estimating how much a particular citation contributes to the later document’s topical content.

The model’s predicted citation influences are evaluated against citations rated manually. Those ratings provide a comparison for assessing whether inferred influence strengths align with human judgments. The abstract reports this evaluation without specifying its outcome. The contribution is a model that connects document topics and citation relationships to the goal of mapping intellectual influence, going beyond displaying citation links without estimates of their strength.
icml-2007-unsupervised-prediction-of-cit.tldr: A probabilistic topic model separates topical innovation from citation-based inheritance to estimate influence between research papers.
